whole_numbers.name: Whole Numbers
whole_numbers.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I help you count your toys or apples: 0, 1, 2, 3!
I start at zero and count upward. I never go below 0!
If you cut a cookie in half, a half piece cannot join me!
I count full things you can touch, like 4 cars or 5 books.
I am any full counting number starting from 0 (0, 1, 2, 3...) with no cuts or dots!
hints: Simple positive counting numbers starting from 0.

educationalInfo.definition: Whole numbers are non-negative numbers starting from 0 without fractional or decimal parts.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking negative numbers or fractions can be whole numbers.
educationalInfo.funFact: Zero was added to counting numbers to form Whole Numbers!

whole_numbers.hint: Focus on non-negative counting numbers starting from 0 (0, 1, 2, 3...) with no fractions or decimals.

integers.name: Integers
integers.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I describe scoreboards, bank money, and weather temperature!
I step both forward into positive numbers and backward into negative numbers!
Even when I go below zero, every step is a full step—no half pieces or dots allowed!
I show freezing cold winter days like 5 degrees below zero (-5)!
I am all positive full numbers, zero, and negative full numbers (..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2,...)!
hints: Includes numbers going both left and right from zero.
Includes positive numbers, zero, and negative numbers.

educationalInfo.definition: Integers are all positive full numbers, negative full numbers, and zero (..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...).
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking integers can include decimals like -2.5.
educationalInfo.funFact: The word 'Integer' comes from Latin and means 'whole' or 'intact'!

integers.hint: Think of positive and negative whole numbers including zero (..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...).

fractions.name: Fractions
fractions.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I appear whenever you share a pizza or slice a birthday cake!
I show parts of a whole thing, sitting between full counting numbers.
I am written with two stacked numbers separated by a flat bar line (like 1/2)—never a decimal dot!
When 4 friends share 1 pizza equally, I show each friend gets 1/4 of the pizza!
I show parts of a whole written with a top number (numerator) and a bottom number (denominator)!
hints: Shows parts of a whole thing.
Has one number on top and one on the bottom.
Uses a slash or horizontal dividing line.

educationalInfo.definition: A fraction represents a part of a whole unit, written as a numerator over a denominator (a/b).
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing numerator (top) and denominator (bottom).
educationalInfo.funFact: The word 'fraction' comes from the Latin word 'fractio', which means 'to break'!

fractions.hint: Recall that a fraction represents a part of a whole unit, written as numerator over denominator.

decimal_numbers.name: Decimal Numbers
decimal_numbers.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I show up on price tags at the store, stopwatch timers, and height rulers!
I show tiny amounts smaller than 1, like cents in money!
I separate whole numbers from tiny parts using a little dot point separator!
You see me every time you buy a juice box for $1.50 or run a race in 10.5 seconds!
I am a number that uses a dot point (decimal point) to show parts smaller than 1!
hints: Shows amounts with a tiny dot.
Uses a decimal point to separate whole units from parts.

educationalInfo.definition: A decimal number uses a decimal point (dot) to separate whole units from fractional place values.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Putting the decimal point in the wrong place.
educationalInfo.funFact: The word 'decimal' comes from the Latin 'decem', meaning 'ten'!

decimal_numbers.hint: Think about numbers that use a decimal point to represent values less than one (tenths, hundredths).

prime_number.name: Prime Number
prime_number.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a special number that cannot be made by multiplying smaller whole numbers together!
I have EXACTLY two factors: 1 and myself!
Numbers like 4, 6, 8, 9 cannot join me because they have extra multiplication partners.
Numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, and 11 are my best friends!
I am a whole number greater than 1 with exactly two factors: 1 and itself!

educationalInfo.definition: A whole number greater than 1 with exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing prime numbers with odd numbers (e.g. 9 or 15 are odd but not prime). Believing 1 is a prime number.
educationalInfo.funFact: The number 2 is the only even prime number. All other prime numbers are odd!
practiceQuestions: Is 29 a prime number?
What is the next prime number after 19?

prime_number.hint: Focus on numbers greater than 1 that have exactly two factors: 1 and themselves (e.g. 2, 3, 5, 7, 11).

composite_number.name: Composite Number
composite_number.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a team number built by multiplying smaller whole numbers together!
I have MORE than two factors (multiplication partners)!
You can arrange my count into equal rows or box grids, like a 2x3 egg box.
Numbers like 4, 6, 8, 9, 10 belong to my team!
I am any positive whole number greater than 1 that has more than two factors!

educationalInfo.definition: A positive integer that has at least one positive divisor other than 1 and itself.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking 1 is composite — it is neither prime nor composite.
educationalInfo.funFact: Every composite number can be uniquely expressed as a product of prime numbers, known as its prime factorisation.
practiceQuestions: List all composite numbers below 20.
Why is 1 neither prime nor composite?

composite_number.hint: Think of positive integers greater than 1 that have more than two positive factors (e.g. 4, 6, 8, 9).

factors.name: Factors
factors.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a smaller number that fits inside a bigger number perfectly!
I divide into a target number cleanly with no remainder left over!
For 12, my family members are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12!
I tell you how many equal rows you can make with a set of tiles.
I am a whole number that divides another number exactly without leaving a remainder.

educationalInfo.definition: Numbers you multiply together to get another number, or numbers that divide a target number exactly.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing factors with multiples (factors are always less than or equal to the target number).
educationalInfo.funFact: Perfect numbers are numbers equal to the sum of their proper factors (e.g., 6 = 1 + 2 + 3).
practiceQuestions: Find all the factors of 18.
What is the greatest factor of 48?

factors.hint: Think about numbers that multiply together to give a specific product.

multiples.name: Multiples
multiples.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am what you get when you skip-count by a number!
I grow bigger and bigger forever as you multiply by 1, 2, 3, 4...
Skip-counting by 5 gives my family: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25...
I tell you when a clock chime or bus arrives on a regular repeating schedule!
I am the result of multiplying a whole number by any counting number!

educationalInfo.definition: The product of a given number and any integer.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing factors with multiples (multiples are infinite and grow larger).
educationalInfo.funFact: Zero is technically a multiple of every number, but we usually ignore it in math practice games.
practiceQuestions: What is the 5th multiple of 9?
Is 45 a multiple of 6?

multiples.hint: Focus on numbers obtained by multiplying a given integer by 1, 2, 3, 4, etc.

lcm.name: LCM
lcm.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I look at two numbers and find the SMALLEST skip-count match they both share!
I help you add fractions with different bottom numbers by finding a shared denominator!
For 4 and 6, skip-counting gives 4, 8, 12... and 6, 12... so 12 is our first meeting point!
I tell you when two blinking lights or flashing signals will flash together again at the exact same moment!
I am the Least Common Multiple—the smallest positive number that is a multiple of two or more numbers!
hints: Used for common denominators in fractions.

educationalInfo.definition: The Least Common Multiple (LCM) is the smallest positive integer divisible by each of the given numbers.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing LCM with HCF.
educationalInfo.funFact: For any two numbers a and b: HCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b!

lcm.hint: Recall the Least Common Multiple — the smallest positive integer divisible by all numbers in a set.

hcf.name: HCF (GCD)
hcf.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I look at two numbers and find the LARGEST common helper that divides both!
I help you simplify big fractions to their simplest form!
For numbers 12 and 18, the numbers that divide both are 1, 2, 3, and 6—and I am the biggest one (6)!
You use me to cut two pieces of wood into the largest equal lengths with zero waste!
I am the Highest Common Factor (or GCD)—the largest number that divides two or more numbers exactly!

educationalInfo.definition: The Highest Common Factor (HCF) is the largest positive integer that divides two or more numbers without remainder.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing HCF (largest factor) with LCM (smallest multiple).
educationalInfo.funFact: If the HCF of two numbers is 1, they are called co-prime numbers!

hcf.hint: Recall the Highest Common Factor (GCD) — the largest number that divides into all given numbers.

fraction.name: Fraction
fraction.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I represent a part of a whole.
I am written with one number above another, separated by a horizontal bar.
My top number is called the numerator.
My bottom number is called the denominator.
When cut a pizza into 4 equal slices and take 3, I am 3/4.

educationalInfo.definition: A number representing a part of a whole, expressed as one integer divided by another.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Adding fractions by adding numerators and denominators separately (e.g. 1/2 + 1/3 ≠ 2/5).
educationalInfo.funFact: Ancient Egyptians only used fractions with numerator 1 (unit fractions). They would write 3/4 as 1/2 + 1/4.
practiceQuestions: Simplify the fraction 12/16.
What is 2/3 + 1/4?

thoughts: I show a part of something.
I like sharing.
I have one number on top.
And one number below.
Half a pizza is my friend.

decimal.name: Decimal
decimal.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a way to write numbers that are not whole.
I use a point to separate whole parts from fractional parts.
Our counting system is Base 10, which is also my name.
The digit immediately to my right of the point represents tenths.
The number 3.14 is a famous example — it approximates pi.

educationalInfo.definition: A number expressed in the base-10 system using a decimal point to separate the whole from the fractional part.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Misaligning decimal points when adding or subtracting. Thinking 0.10 and 0.1 are different numbers.
educationalInfo.funFact: The decimal system was popularised in Europe by Simon Stevin in 1585, though India used it centuries earlier.
practiceQuestions: Convert 3/4 into a decimal.
What is 1.5 + 2.75?

thoughts: I have a little dot.
I can be smaller than one.
Money likes me.
5.25 is one of my friends.
My dot is very important.

percentage.name: Percentages
percentage.subject: Arithmetic Kingdom
clues: I tell how much of a whole you have.
Shops use me during discounts and sales.
Exam marks are often written using me.
I mean "out of every 100."
I am written using the % symbol.
thoughts: I tell how much of a whole you have.
Shops use me during discounts and sales.
Exam marks are often written using me.
I mean "out of every 100."
I am written using the % symbol.

educationalInfo.definition: A rate, number, or amount in each hundred; a fraction expressed as a portion of 100.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting to divide by 100 when converting percentage to a decimal.

percentage.hint: Recall that Percentages refers to: A rate, number, or amount in each hundred; a fraction expressed as a portion of 100.

integer.name: Integer
integer.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am a complete number — no fractions, no decimals.
I include both positive and negative whole numbers.
I also include zero.
The set of me extends infinitely in both directions on a number line.

educationalInfo.definition: Any whole number (positive, negative, or zero) — not a fraction or decimal.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking negative numbers are not integers, or that fractions can be integers.
educationalInfo.funFact: The word integer comes from the Latin 'integer' meaning 'whole' or 'untouched'.
practiceQuestions: Is -7 an integer?
List three negative integers greater than -5.

integer.hint: Recall that Integer refers to: Any whole number (positive, negative, or zero) — not a fraction or decimal.

right_triangle.name: Right Triangle
right_triangle.subject: Geometry
clues: I am a three-sided flat shape.
One of my interior angles measures exactly 90 degrees.
My longest side has a special name: the hypotenuse.
My area can be computed simply as half times base times height.
Trigonometry is built on my ratios.

educationalInfo.definition: A triangle in which one angle is a right angle (90 degrees).
examples: A triangle with angles 30, 60, and 90 degrees.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Assuming the right angle is always at the bottom-left corner.
educationalInfo.funFact: A right triangle can also be isosceles, with angles 45, 45, and 90 degrees.
practiceQuestions: Can a triangle have two right angles?
If a right triangle has an angle of 40 degrees, what is the third angle?

right_triangle.hint: Recall that Right Triangle refers to: A triangle in which one angle is a right angle (90 degrees).

pythagoras_theorem.name: Pythagoras' Theorem
pythagoras_theorem.subject: Geometry
clues: I am a famous geometric principle.
I apply strictly to right-angled triangles.
I state that the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of squares of the other two sides.
My algebraic formula is written as a^2 + b^2 = c^2.
Numbers like (3, 4, 5) and (5, 12, 13) are my triples.

educationalInfo.definition: A fundamental relation in Euclidean geometry: a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse of a right triangle.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Applying the formula to non-right triangles. Incorrectly squaring sides (e.g. thinking a + b = c).
educationalInfo.funFact: Ancient Babylonian, Indian, and Chinese mathematicians knew this relationship centuries before Pythagoras.
practiceQuestions: If the legs of a right triangle are 6 and 8, find the hypotenuse.
Is a triangle with side lengths 7, 24, and 25 a right triangle?

pythagoras_theorem.hint: Recall that Pythagoras' Theorem refers to: A fundamental relation in Euclidean geometry: a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse of a right triangle.

perimeter.name: Perimeter
perimeter.subject: Geometry
clues: I represent a boundary measurement.
I measure the total continuous distance around the outside of a 2D shape.
For a circle, my value is called the circumference.
For a polygon, you calculate me by adding all side lengths together.
For a square of side s, my formula is 4s.

educationalInfo.definition: The continuous line forming the boundary of a closed two-dimensional shape.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing perimeter with area (perimeter is linear length, not square units).
educationalInfo.funFact: The word perimeter comes from the Greek 'peri' (around) and 'metron' (measure).
practiceQuestions: Calculate the perimeter of a regular hexagon with side length 5cm.
What is the perimeter of a rectangle with length 10m and width 4m?

perimeter.hint: Recall that Perimeter refers to: The continuous line forming the boundary of a closed two-dimensional shape.

area.name: Area
area.subject: Geometry
clues: I measure two-dimensional space.
I count the amount of square units needed to cover a flat surface.
For a rectangle, my value is length multiplied by width.
For a circle, my formula is pi times radius squared.
My units are written with a superscript 2, such as square meters.

educationalInfo.definition: The quantity that expresses the extent of a two-dimensional figure in the plane.
examples: Area of a square with side 5cm = 25 cm².
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Measuring area in linear units instead of square units. Confusing perimeter and area formulas.
educationalInfo.funFact: A standard A4 sheet of paper has an area of exactly 1/16th of a square meter.
practiceQuestions: Find the area of a triangle with base 8cm and height 5cm.
If a square has a perimeter of 24cm, what is its area?

area.hint: Recall that Area refers to: The quantity that expresses the extent of a two-dimensional figure in the plane.

volume.name: Volume
volume.subject: Geometry
clues: I measure three-dimensional capacity.
I count the amount of cubic space occupied by a solid object.
For a cuboid, my calculation is length × width × height.
For a cylinder, my formula is pi × r² × h.
My units are written with a superscript 3, such as cm³ or cubic meters.

educationalInfo.definition: The amount of three-dimensional space enclosed by a closed surface.
examples: Volume of a cube with side 3cm = 27 cm³.
A cylinder with radius 2cm and height 5cm has volume ≈ 62.8 cm³.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Using area formulas instead of multiplying by height. Measuring volume in square units.
educationalInfo.funFact: One litre is defined as the volume of a cube that measures 10cm on each side (1000 cm³).
practiceQuestions: Calculate the volume of a box measuring 5cm × 4cm × 3cm.
What is the volume of a sphere of radius 3 units (in terms of pi)?

volume.hint: Recall that Volume refers to: The amount of three-dimensional space enclosed by a closed surface.

circle.name: Circle
circle.subject: Geometry
clues: I am a perfectly round shape.
Every point on my boundary is exactly the same distance from my centre.
That fixed distance is called my radius.
My boundary length is called my circumference, equal to 2πr.
The constant π (pi) is the ratio of my circumference to my diameter.

educationalInfo.definition: A round plane figure whose boundary consists of points equidistant from a fixed centre point.
examples: A coin is a circular shape.
The face of a clock is a circle with radius ≈ 10cm.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing radius with diameter (diameter = 2 × radius).
educationalInfo.funFact: A circle has the largest area of any 2D shape with a given perimeter — this is why bubbles are spherical.
practiceQuestions: Find the circumference of a circle with radius 7cm.
What is the area of a circle with diameter 10cm?

circle.hint: Recall that Circle refers to: A round plane figure whose boundary consists of points equidistant from a fixed centre point.

polygon.name: Polygon
polygon.subject: Geometry
clues: I am a closed flat shape made entirely of straight sides.
My name comes from Greek meaning 'many angles'.
Triangles, squares, and hexagons are all examples of me.
A regular version of me has all sides and angles equal.
The sum of my interior angles is (n-2) × 180 degrees, where n is my number of sides.

educationalInfo.definition: A plane figure with at least three straight sides and angles.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Including circles or shapes with curved sides as polygons.
educationalInfo.funFact: A polygon with a million sides (a megagon) looks indistinguishable from a circle to the naked eye.
practiceQuestions: What is the sum of interior angles of a pentagon?
What is a polygon with 8 sides called?

polygon.hint: Recall that Polygon refers to: A plane figure with at least three straight sides and angles.

cylinder.name: Cylinder
cylinder.subject: Geometry
clues: I am a three-dimensional solid shape.
I have two circular faces that are parallel and identical.
A rectangular surface wraps around my sides.
My volume is calculated as pi times radius squared times height.
A tin can or a battery is a real-world example of me.

educationalInfo.definition: A three-dimensional solid with two parallel circular bases connected by a curved lateral surface.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Using the diameter instead of the radius in the volume formula.
educationalInfo.funFact: Cylinders are incredibly strong structures — the cylindrical shape of columns can hold enormous weight.
practiceQuestions: Find the volume of a cylinder with radius 3cm and height 10cm.
What is the surface area of a cylinder with r=5 and h=8?

cylinder.hint: Recall that Cylinder refers to: A three-dimensional solid with two parallel circular bases connected by a curved lateral surface.

coordinate.name: Coordinate
coordinate.subject: Geometry
clues: I am a set of numbers that describe a position.
I am used to locate a point on a grid or in space.
On a 2D plane, I come in ordered pairs like (x, y).
The origin of my system is at point (0, 0).
René Descartes invented the system I belong to, called the Cartesian system.

educationalInfo.definition: A pair (or set) of numbers used to indicate the position of a point on a graph or in space.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Swapping x and y values — always read (horizontal, vertical).
educationalInfo.funFact: Legend says Descartes invented his coordinate system while watching a fly on his ceiling, wondering how to describe its position.
practiceQuestions: Plot the point (4, -2) on a coordinate grid.
What coordinate is at the origin?

coordinate.hint: Recall that Coordinate refers to: A pair (or set) of numbers used to indicate the position of a point on a graph or in space.

sphere.name: Sphere
sphere.subject: Geometry
clues: I am the 3D version of a circle.
Every point on my surface is equidistant from my centre.
My volume is calculated as (4/3) × pi × radius cubed.
A ball, globe, and bubble are all examples of me.
I have no edges, no vertices, and only one curved surface.

educationalInfo.definition: A perfectly round geometrical object in three-dimensional space that is the set of all points equidistant from a given centre.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing a sphere (solid) with a circle (flat 2D). Using area formula instead of volume formula.
educationalInfo.funFact: Of all 3D shapes, a sphere has the smallest surface area for a given volume — which is why planets are spherical.
practiceQuestions: Find the volume of a sphere with radius 6cm.
What is the surface area of a sphere (formula)?

sphere.hint: Recall that Sphere refers to: A perfectly round geometrical object in three-dimensional space that is the set of all points equidistant from a given centre.

variable.name: Variable
variable.subject: Algebra
clues: I am a basic building block of algebra.
I represent a quantity whose value is unknown or can change.
I am usually written as a letter from the alphabet.
The letters x, y, and z are my most common representatives.
In the term 5x, I am represented by the x.

educationalInfo.definition: A symbol (usually a letter) standing for an unknown numerical value in an equation or algebraic expression.
examples: In y = mx + c, x and y are variables.
In x + 2 = 5, x is the variable.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Treating variables as constants. Forgetting that different variables represent different values.
educationalInfo.funFact: René Descartes introduced the convention of using x, y, z for variables and a, b, c for constants.
practiceQuestions: Identify the variable in the expression 3a - 7.
Can a variable take multiple values in a function?

variable.hint: Recall that Variable refers to: A symbol (usually a letter) standing for an unknown numerical value in an equation or algebraic expression.

expression.name: Expression
expression.subject: Algebra
clues: I combine terms using math operations.
I contain numbers, variables, and operation symbols.
Unlike an equation, I do NOT contain an equals sign.
I can be simplified, but I cannot be solved on my own.
An example of my form is 3x + 2y - 7.

educationalInfo.definition: A mathematical phrase containing numbers, variables, and operators — but no equality sign.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing an expression with an equation (equations have '=', expressions do not).
educationalInfo.funFact: Expressions are the algebraic equivalent of a sentence fragment, while equations are complete sentences.
practiceQuestions: Simplify the expression: 2x + 3x - 4.
Is '5x + 3 = 13' an expression or an equation?

expression.hint: Recall that Expression refers to: A mathematical phrase containing numbers, variables, and operators — but no equality sign.

linear_equation.name: Linear Equation
linear_equation.subject: Algebra
clues: I am an algebraic statement of equality.
My graph forms a straight line.
The highest exponent of my variables is exactly 1.
My standard form is written as y = mx + c.
An example of my form is 2x + 5 = 11.

educationalInfo.definition: An equation between two variables that gives a straight line when plotted on a graph.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking equations with variables squared are linear. Forgetting to apply operations to both sides.
educationalInfo.funFact: Linear equations are the foundation of linear programming, used to optimize shipping and logistics.
practiceQuestions: Solve for x: 3x - 4 = 11.
Does the point (2, 5) lie on the line y = 2x + 1?

linear_equation.hint: Recall that Linear Equation refers to: An equation between two variables that gives a straight line when plotted on a graph.

quadratic_equation.name: Quadratic Equation
quadratic_equation.subject: Algebra
clues: I am an algebraic relation.
My graph forms a U-shaped curve called a parabola.
The highest exponent of my variable is exactly 2.
My standard form is ax² + bx + c = 0.
My solutions can be found using factorisation, completing the square, or the quadratic formula.

educationalInfo.definition: Any equation that can be rearranged in standard form as ax² + bx + c = 0, where a ≠ 0.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting the ± sign when taking square roots. Missing the quadratic term when rearranging.
educationalInfo.funFact: The path of any thrown object — a basketball or a stone — is a parabola described by a quadratic equation.
practiceQuestions: Find the roots of x² - 9 = 0.
How many solutions does x² - 4x + 4 = 0 have?

quadratic_equation.hint: Recall that Quadratic Equation refers to: Any equation that can be rearranged in standard form as ax² + bx + c = 0, where a ≠ 0.

inequality.name: Inequality
inequality.subject: Algebra
clues: I describe a comparison between two mathematical quantities.
I show that one value is larger or smaller than another.
I use symbols that resemble arrowheads or wedges.
When you multiply both sides by a negative number, you must flip my symbol.
Examples of my symbols are <, >, ≤, and ≥.

educationalInfo.definition: A mathematical statement indicating that one expression is greater than, less than, or not equal to another.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting to flip the inequality sign when dividing or multiplying by a negative number.
educationalInfo.funFact: The '<' and '>' symbols were introduced by mathematician Thomas Harriot in 1631.
practiceQuestions: Solve for x: -2x > 8.
Represent x ≥ 3 on a number line.

inequality.hint: Recall that Inequality refers to: A mathematical statement indicating that one expression is greater than, less than, or not equal to another.

ratio.name: Ratio
ratio.subject: Arithmetic Kingdom
clues: I compare two quantities.
Recipes often use me.
Maps and scale drawings also use me.
I tell how much of one thing there is compared to another.
I am written using the : symbol.
thoughts: I compare two quantities.
Recipes often use me.
Maps and scale drawings also use me.
I tell how much of one thing there is compared to another.
I am written using the : symbol.

educationalInfo.definition: The quantitative relation between two amounts showing the number of times one value contains or is contained within the other.
examples: Ratio of flour to sugar is 2:1
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Adding ratios together directly or reversing the order of terms.

ratio.hint: Recall that Ratio refers to: The quantitative relation between two amounts showing the number of times one value contains or is contained within the other.

sequence.name: Sequence
sequence.subject: Algebra
clues: I am an ordered list of numbers following a rule.
Each number in me is called a term.
I can be arithmetic (constant difference) or geometric (constant ratio).
Fibonacci created a famous version of me: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8...
If my terms increase by 3 each time starting from 2, I am 2, 5, 8, 11...

educationalInfo.definition: An ordered list of numbers (terms) following a defined rule or pattern.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing arithmetic sequences (addition) with geometric sequences (multiplication).
educationalInfo.funFact: The Fibonacci sequence (1,1,2,3,5,8...) appears in the spirals of sunflowers, pinecones, and galaxies.
practiceQuestions: Find the 7th term of the arithmetic sequence 4, 7, 10...
What type of sequence is 2, 4, 8, 16?

sequence.hint: Recall that Sequence refers to: An ordered list of numbers (terms) following a defined rule or pattern.

function.name: Function
function.subject: Algebra
clues: I am a special rule that maps each input to exactly one output.
I am often written using f(x) notation.
I can be pictured as a machine: input goes in, output comes out.
On a graph, I pass the vertical line test — any vertical line crosses me at most once.
f(x) = 2x + 3 means for any x, my output is double x plus 3.

educationalInfo.definition: A rule that assigns exactly one output value to each input value.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking a relation where one input gives multiple outputs is a function (it is not).
educationalInfo.funFact: Functions are the backbone of all computer programming — every program is ultimately a chain of functions.
practiceQuestions: If f(x) = 3x - 2, find f(4).
Is y = ±√x a function? Why or why not?

function.hint: Recall that Function refers to: A rule that assigns exactly one output value to each input value.

gradient.name: Gradient
gradient.subject: Algebra
clues: I measure the steepness of a line.
I am defined as rise divided by run.
A horizontal line has me equal to zero.
A vertical line has me as undefined.
In the equation y = mx + c, I am represented by the letter m.

educationalInfo.definition: The steepness or slope of a line, measured as the ratio of vertical change (rise) to horizontal change (run).
examples: A line through (0,0) and (2,4) has gradient 4/2 = 2.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Dividing run by rise instead of rise by run.
educationalInfo.funFact: Road gradients are expressed as percentages — a '10% gradient' means you rise 10m for every 100m you travel forward.
practiceQuestions: Find the gradient of the line through (1,2) and (3,6).
What is the gradient of y = -5x + 7?

gradient.hint: Recall that Gradient refers to: The steepness or slope of a line, measured as the ratio of vertical change (rise) to horizontal change (run).

matrix.name: Matrix
matrix.subject: Algebra
clues: I am a rectangular arrangement of numbers.
I organise my elements into rows and columns.
My size is described by rows × columns (e.g. a 2×3 has 2 rows and 3 columns).
Two of me can be multiplied only when the columns of the first equal the rows of the second.
I am used in computer graphics, machine learning, and physics simulations.

educationalInfo.definition: A rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns, used to represent linear transformations.
examples: An identity matrix has 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Trying to add matrices of different dimensions. Swapping rows and columns (that gives the transpose).
educationalInfo.funFact: Google's original PageRank algorithm was solved using a massive matrix operation over the entire web graph.
practiceQuestions: What is the order of a matrix with 3 rows and 2 columns?
Can you add a 2×3 matrix to a 3×2 matrix?

matrix.hint: Recall that Matrix refers to: A rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns, used to represent linear transformations.

mean.name: Mean
mean.subject: Statistics
clues: I am a measure of central tendency.
People often call me the average.
To find me, you must sum all values in a dataset.
After summing, you divide by the total count of numbers.
For the dataset {2, 4, 9}, my value is 5.

educationalInfo.definition: The average value of a set of numbers, calculated by dividing the sum of the values by their count.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting to divide by the count of items. Getting skewed results from outliers.
educationalInfo.funFact: The arithmetic mean is just one type of mean; others include the geometric mean and harmonic mean.
practiceQuestions: Find the mean of {5, 8, 11, 16}.
If the sum of 5 numbers is 100, what is their mean?

mean.hint: Recall that Mean refers to: The average value of a set of numbers, calculated by dividing the sum of the values by their count.

median.name: Median
median.subject: Statistics
clues: I represent the middle point of a dataset.
Before finding me, you must sort the numbers in ascending order.
If the count is odd, I am exactly the middle number.
If the count is even, I am the mean of the two middle numbers.
For the sorted dataset {1, 3, 7, 10}, my value is 5.

educationalInfo.definition: The middle number in a sorted, ascending or descending list of numbers.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting to sort the numbers before picking the middle value.
educationalInfo.funFact: Unlike the mean, the median is robust to outliers — which is why median house prices are reported instead of average prices.
practiceQuestions: Find the median of {12, 3, 8, 15, 6}.
What is the median of {1, 2, 9, 10}?

median.hint: Recall that Median refers to: The middle number in a sorted, ascending or descending list of numbers.

mode.name: Mode
mode.subject: Statistics
clues: I am the most popular member of a dataset.
I measure the value that appears with the highest frequency.
A dataset can have one of me, multiple of me, or none at all.
I am the only average that can be used for descriptive words (categorical data).
For the dataset {2, 3, 3, 4, 5}, my value is 3.

educationalInfo.definition: The value that appears most frequently in a data set.
examples: Mode of {blue, red, blue, green} is blue.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking a dataset must have exactly one mode. Confusing frequency with the value itself.
educationalInfo.funFact: The word mode comes from the French 'la mode', meaning fashion — i.e., what is most popular.
practiceQuestions: What is the mode of {5, 7, 5, 8, 7, 5}?
Can a set of numbers have no mode?

mode.hint: Recall that Mode refers to: The value that appears most frequently in a data set.

range.name: Range
range.subject: Statistics
clues: I am the simplest measure of spread in a dataset.
I describe how spread out the data values are.
I am calculated by subtracting the smallest value from the largest.
A small value of me means the data is clustered closely together.
For the dataset {3, 7, 12, 20}, my value is 17.

educationalInfo.definition: The difference between the largest and smallest values in a dataset, measuring spread.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Subtracting the largest from the smallest (giving a negative result). Confusing range with mean.
educationalInfo.funFact: Meteorologists report daily temperature range as the difference between the day's highest and lowest temperatures.
practiceQuestions: Find the range of {8, 3, 15, 6, 11}.
If range is 12 and the minimum is 5, what is the maximum?

range.hint: Recall that Range refers to: The difference between the largest and smallest values in a dataset, measuring spread.

probability.name: Probability
probability.subject: Statistics
clues: I measure likelihood and chance.
My value always lies strictly between 0 and 1 (inclusive).
A value of 0 means impossible, while 1 means absolute certainty.
I am computed as successful outcomes divided by total outcomes.
The chance of rolling a 4 on a standard six-sided die is 1/6.

educationalInfo.definition: The branch of mathematics concerning numerical descriptions of how likely an event is to occur.
examples: Probability of heads on a coin flip = 0.5.
Drawing an ace from a deck = 4/52 = 1/13.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Expressing probability as a number greater than 1. Confusing odds (1 to 3) with probability (1/4).
educationalInfo.funFact: Modern probability theory was developed in the 17th century by Pascal and Fermat to solve gambling problems.
practiceQuestions: What is the probability of rolling an even number on a die?
If a bag has 3 red and 7 blue marbles, what is the probability of picking red?

probability.hint: Recall that Probability refers to: The branch of mathematics concerning numerical descriptions of how likely an event is to occur.

venn_diagram.name: Venn Diagram
venn_diagram.subject: Statistics
clues: I am a visual way to show collections.
I represent mathematical sets and their relationships.
I consist of overlapping circles drawn inside a rectangular box.
The overlapping section represents the intersection of sets.
John Venn created me in 1880.

educationalInfo.definition: An illustration using overlapping circles to show relationships among groups of things.
examples: A diagram showing common multiples of 2 and 3 in the overlap.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting to include elements that belong outside both circles inside the universal set rectangle.
educationalInfo.funFact: The rectangular bounding box representing the universal set is mathematically required but often omitted in popular memes.
practiceQuestions: If set A has 5 items, B has 4, and they overlap by 2, what is |A ∪ B|?
What does the overlapping area in a Venn diagram represent?

venn_diagram.hint: Recall that Venn Diagram refers to: An illustration using overlapping circles to show relationships among groups of things.

set.name: Set
set.subject: Statistics
clues: I am a well-defined collection of distinct objects.
My members are called elements.
I am written using curly braces with elements separated by commas.
The size of me is called my cardinality.
The empty version of me is written as {} or the symbol ∅.

educationalInfo.definition: A well-defined collection of distinct objects, considered as an object in its own right.
examples: {1, 2, 3} is a set of three integers.
{a, e, i, o, u} is the set of vowels.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Allowing duplicate elements — a set can only contain each element once.
educationalInfo.funFact: Set theory, developed by Georg Cantor in the 1870s, is the foundation of all modern mathematics.
practiceQuestions: What is the union of {1,2,3} and {3,4,5}?
What is the intersection of {a,b,c} and {b,c,d}?

set.hint: Recall that Set refers to: A well-defined collection of distinct objects, considered as an object in its own right.

standard_deviation.name: Standard Deviation
standard_deviation.subject: Statistics
clues: I measure how spread out data is from the mean.
A small value of me means data points are clustered close to the average.
A large value of me means data is more dispersed.
I am the square root of the variance.
I am symbolised by the Greek letter sigma (σ).

educationalInfo.definition: A measure of the amount of variation or dispersion of a set of values from their mean.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing standard deviation with range. Forgetting to take the square root of variance.
educationalInfo.funFact: In a normal distribution, about 68% of data falls within 1 standard deviation of the mean, and 95% within 2.
practiceQuestions: If variance = 25, what is the standard deviation?
Which dataset has greater spread: {5,5,5} or {2,5,8}?

standard_deviation.hint: Recall that Standard Deviation refers to: A measure of the amount of variation or dispersion of a set of values from their mean.

normal_distribution.name: Normal Distribution
normal_distribution.subject: Statistics
clues: I am a symmetric bell-shaped curve.
My peak sits exactly at the mean.
Most values cluster around my centre, with fewer values at the extremes.
I am completely described by just two values: mean and standard deviation.
Heights, IQ scores, and exam marks often follow my shape.

educationalInfo.definition: A probability distribution that is symmetric about the mean, forming a bell-shaped curve.
examples: Heights of adult males in a population.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Assuming all real-world data follows a normal distribution. Forgetting it is symmetric around the mean, not the median.
educationalInfo.funFact: Carl Friedrich Gauss studied this distribution so extensively it is also called the Gaussian distribution.
practiceQuestions: In a normal distribution, what percentage of data lies within 1 SD of the mean?
If mean = 50 and SD = 10, between what values does 95% of data fall?

normal_distribution.hint: Recall that Normal Distribution refers to: A probability distribution that is symmetric about the mean, forming a bell-shaped curve.

scatter_graph.name: Scatter Graph
scatter_graph.subject: Statistics
clues: I am a type of statistical graph.
I plot pairs of values as individual dots.
I am used to investigate the relationship between two variables.
A line of best fit can be drawn through my points.
Positive correlation means my dots rise from left to right.

educationalInfo.definition: A graph using dots to represent values for two different variables, showing possible correlations.
examples: Plotting height vs weight for a class of students.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing correlation with causation — just because two things correlate does not mean one causes the other.
educationalInfo.funFact: Scatter graphs were first used by Francis Galton in the 1880s to study the relationship between parents' and children's heights.
practiceQuestions: What does a scatter graph with all points on a perfect line indicate?
Describe the correlation if dots fall from top-left to bottom-right.

scatter_graph.hint: Recall that Scatter Graph refers to: A graph using dots to represent values for two different variables, showing possible correlations.

sine.name: Sine
sine.subject: Trigonometry
clues: I am a basic trigonometric function.
In a right triangle, I equal the length of the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse.
My value for a 30-degree angle is exactly 0.5.
My graph oscillates continuously between -1 and +1.
My mathematical abbreviation is sin.

educationalInfo.definition: The trigonometric function equal to opposite ÷ hypotenuse for an acute angle in a right triangle.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Dividing adjacent by hypotenuse instead of opposite by hypotenuse. Forgetting Degree mode on calculator.
educationalInfo.funFact: The word sine originates from a Latin mistranslation of the Arabic word 'jaib', meaning pocket or fold.
practiceQuestions: What is the value of sin(0)?
If opposite = 5 and hypotenuse = 10, find sin of the angle.

sine.hint: Recall that Sine refers to: The trigonometric function equal to opposite ÷ hypotenuse for an acute angle in a right triangle.

cosine.name: Cosine
cosine.subject: Trigonometry
clues: I am a key trigonometric ratio.
In a right triangle, I equal the length of the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse.
My value for a 60-degree angle is exactly 0.5.
At 0 degrees, my value is at its maximum of 1.
My mathematical abbreviation is cos.

educationalInfo.definition: The trigonometric function equal to adjacent ÷ hypotenuse for an acute angle in a right triangle.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Using the opposite side instead of the adjacent side in calculations.
educationalInfo.funFact: The cosine of an angle is identical to the sine of its complementary angle — hence the 'co-' prefix.
practiceQuestions: What is the value of cos(90°)?
If adjacent = 4 and hypotenuse = 5, find the cosine.

cosine.hint: Recall that Cosine refers to: The trigonometric function equal to adjacent ÷ hypotenuse for an acute angle in a right triangle.

tangent.name: Tangent
tangent.subject: Trigonometry
clues: I represent a ratio of triangle legs.
In a right triangle, I equal the opposite side divided by the adjacent side.
I can also be calculated as sine divided by cosine.
My value for a 45-degree angle is exactly 1.
My mathematical abbreviation is tan.

educationalInfo.definition: A trigonometric function representing opposite ÷ adjacent in a right triangle.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Inverting the ratio (dividing adjacent by opposite gives cotangent, not tangent).
educationalInfo.funFact: At 90°, tangent is undefined because cosine is 0 — its graph shoots off to infinity.
practiceQuestions: What is tan(0°)?
Find tan if opposite = 8 and adjacent = 8.

tangent.hint: Recall that Tangent refers to: A trigonometric function representing opposite ÷ adjacent in a right triangle.

hypotenuse.name: Hypotenuse
hypotenuse.subject: Trigonometry
clues: I am a physical component of a right triangle.
I am always the longest side of the triangle.
I am always positioned directly opposite the 90-degree right angle.
In Pythagoras' formula a² + b² = c², I am represented by the letter c.
I serve as the denominator in both sine and cosine calculations.

educationalInfo.definition: The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.
examples: In a 3-4-5 right triangle, the side of length 5 is the hypotenuse.
The diagonal of a rectangle acts as the hypotenuse.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Assuming the hypotenuse is the base or height. Applying the term to non-right-angle triangles.
educationalInfo.funFact: The word hypotenuse comes from the Greek 'hypoteinousa', meaning 'stretching under'.
practiceQuestions: In a right triangle with legs 5 and 12, what is the hypotenuse?
Which side is the hypotenuse in a triangle with angles 40°, 50°, 90°?

hypotenuse.hint: Recall that Hypotenuse refers to: The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.

angle_of_elevation.name: Angle of Elevation
angle_of_elevation.subject: Trigonometry
clues: I measure an upwards line of sight.
I am formed between the horizontal ground and a target point above.
I look upwards, whereas my partner the angle of depression looks down.
I am equal to the angle of depression due to alternate interior angles.
You measure me when looking up at the top of a tree or building.

educationalInfo.definition: The angle formed by the line of sight and the horizontal plane for an object above the horizontal.
examples: Looking up at a bird in a tree.
Measuring the angle from the ground to the top of a flag pole.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Measuring the angle from the vertical instead of the horizontal ground.
educationalInfo.funFact: Surveyors use an instrument called a clinometer or theodolite to measure angles of elevation.
practiceQuestions: If you stand 10m away from a tree and look up at 45°, how tall is the tree?
Explain the difference between angle of elevation and depression.

angle_of_elevation.hint: Recall that Angle of Elevation refers to: The angle formed by the line of sight and the horizontal plane for an object above the horizontal.

vector.name: Vector
vector.subject: Trigonometry
clues: I have both magnitude and direction.
Unlike a scalar, I cannot be fully described by just a number.
I am drawn as an arrow.
In 2D, I am written as a column with x and y components.
Wind speed and velocity are real-world examples of me.

educationalInfo.definition: A quantity that has both magnitude (size) and direction, represented as an arrow.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing vector with scalar. Adding vectors by adding only magnitudes (direction must be considered).
educationalInfo.funFact: GPS navigation constantly uses vector mathematics to calculate the direction and distance to your destination.
practiceQuestions: What is the resultant of vectors (3,4) and (-1,2)?
Give two examples of scalar quantities and two of vector quantities.

vector.hint: Recall that Vector refers to: A quantity that has both magnitude (size) and direction, represented as an arrow.

square_root.name: Square Root
square_root.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am an inverse mathematical operation.
I ask: 'What number multiplied by itself equals the given value?'
I am written with a radical symbol √. The square root of 25 is 5.
Finding the side length of a square room if you know its area is 25 sq meters.
The square root (√) of a number is a value that, when multiplied by itself, gives the original number.

educationalInfo.definition: The square root (√) of a number is a value that, when multiplied by itself, yields the original number.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Dividing by 2 instead of finding the square root.
educationalInfo.funFact: Square root of 2 (√2 ≈ 1.414) was the first irrational number discovered!

square_root.hint: Recall that Square Root refers to: The square root (√) of a number is a value that, when multiplied by itself, yields the original number.

cube_root.name: Cube Root
cube_root.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am an inverse operation used in 3D geometry.
I ask: 'What number multiplied by itself three times equals the given value?'
I am written with a radical symbol with a small 3 (∛). The cube root of 8 is 2.
Finding the side length of a cube box if you know its volume is 8 cubic meters.
The cube root (∛) of a number is a value that, when multiplied by itself three times, gives the original number.

educationalInfo.definition: The cube root (∛) of a number is a value that, when multiplied by itself twice, yields the target number.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing square root and cube root.
educationalInfo.funFact: The cube root of a volume gives the side length of a 3D cube!

cube_root.hint: Recall that Cube Root refers to: The cube root (∛) of a number is a value that, when multiplied by itself twice, yields the target number.

square.name: Square (Power)
square.subject: Trigonometry
clues: I am the result of multiplying a number by itself.
I am also written using the exponent 2.
I am always non-negative for real numbers.
4 squared equals 16, and 10 squared equals 100.
My inverse operation is the square root.

educationalInfo.definition: A number multiplied by itself, equivalent to raising a number to the power of 2.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking (-3)² = -9. (It equals +9 because negative × negative = positive.)
educationalInfo.funFact: The numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, 25... are called perfect squares because they are squares of whole numbers.
practiceQuestions: What is 12²?
Is 50 a perfect square?

square.hint: Recall that Square (Power) refers to: A number multiplied by itself, equivalent to raising a number to the power of 2.

cube.name: Cube (Power)
cube.subject: Trigonometry
clues: I am the result of multiplying a number by itself three times.
I am also written using the exponent 3.
The volume of a cube-shaped box is my practical application.
2 cubed equals 8, and 3 cubed equals 27.
My inverse operation is the cube root.

educationalInfo.definition: A number raised to the power of 3, equivalent to multiplying it by itself three times.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing 3² (9) with 2³ (8). Forgetting that negative cubes stay negative.
educationalInfo.funFact: The numbers 1, 8, 27, 64, 125... are called perfect cubes. Ramanujan noticed that 1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³.
practiceQuestions: What is 5³?
Calculate (-3)³.

cube.hint: Recall that Cube (Power) refers to: A number raised to the power of 3, equivalent to multiplying it by itself three times.

addition.name: Addition
addition.subject: Number
clues: I am the most fundamental arithmetic operation.
I combine two or more quantities into a single total.
My symbol is the plus sign (+).
The result of my operation is called the sum.
5 + 3 = 8 is a simple example of me.

educationalInfo.definition: The arithmetic operation of combining two or more numbers to find their total.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Carrying errors when adding multi-digit numbers. Forgetting to align place values.
educationalInfo.funFact: The + symbol was first used in a German manuscript in 1489 by Johannes Widmann.
practiceQuestions: What is 47 + 58?

thoughts: I help numbers come together.
I make the answer bigger.
I use the + sign.
3 + 4 = 7 is my work.
You use me to find the total.

column_addition.name: Column Addition
column_addition.subject: Number
clues: I am a written method for adding large numbers.
I organise digits into columns by their place value.
I process ones first, then tens, then hundreds.
I introduce the concept of carrying a digit to the next column.
Adding 347 + 285 using me gives 632.

educationalInfo.definition: A written method of addition where numbers are aligned vertically by place value, adding column by column from right to left.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting to carry. Misaligning digits in the wrong column.
educationalInfo.funFact: Column addition is one of the oldest written calculation methods, used since medieval Europe.
practiceQuestions: Calculate 456 + 378 using column addition.
Add 1247 + 863 using the column method.

thoughts: I like numbers in a straight line.
One number goes under another.
Ones stay with ones. Tens stay with tens.
Sometimes I carry a number.
I help add big numbers.
column_addition.hint: Write the numbers one below another.

subtraction.name: Subtraction
subtraction.subject: Number
clues: I am the inverse operation of addition.
I find the difference between two quantities.
My symbol is the minus sign (−).
The result of my operation is called the difference.
10 − 3 = 7 is a simple example of me.

educationalInfo.definition: The arithmetic operation of finding the difference between two numbers by removing one quantity from another.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Borrowing errors in column subtraction. Subtracting in the wrong order (larger minus smaller in each column).
educationalInfo.funFact: Subtraction was known to ancient Egyptians and Babylonians — carved into clay tablets over 4000 years ago.
practiceQuestions: What is 73 − 28?
Subtract 456 from 1000.

thoughts: I make numbers smaller.
I take one number away.
I like numbers in a straight line.
Sometimes I borrow.
I help find the difference.

multiplication.name: Multiplication
multiplication.subject: Number
clues: I am a shortcut for repeated addition.
I scale one number by another.
My symbol is × or a dot.
The result of my operation is called the product.
6 × 7 = 42 is a famous example that students memorise.

educationalInfo.definition: An arithmetic operation that scales one number by another, equivalent to repeated addition.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Errors in the times tables. Forgetting to multiply every partial product in long multiplication.
educationalInfo.funFact: The × symbol was introduced by William Oughtred in 1631 — before that, multiplication was written out in words.
practiceQuestions: What is 8 × 9?
Multiply 24 × 15.

thoughts: I like equal groups.
I help count faster.
I use the × sign.
5 × 3 = 15 is my work.
I save you from adding again and again.

column_multiplication.name: Column Multiplication
column_multiplication.subject: Number
clues: I am the written long-multiplication method.
I multiply digit by digit, keeping track of place values.
I generate partial products that are then summed.
I am essential when multiplying two multi-digit numbers.
Multiplying 47 × 23 using me gives 1081.

educationalInfo.definition: A written method for multiplying multi-digit numbers by computing partial products aligned by place value.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting to shift the second partial product left by one place. Errors in individual digit products.
educationalInfo.funFact: The long multiplication algorithm dates back to medieval Islamic mathematics and was formalized by al-Khwarizmi.
practiceQuestions: Calculate 36 × 24 using column multiplication.
Multiply 125 × 32.

thoughts: I like numbers in a straight line.
I multiply one step at a time.
I write small answers first.
Then I add them.
I help multiply big numbers.

hcf_lcm.name: HCF & LCM
hcf_lcm.subject: Number
clues: I cover two closely related number operations.
One of me is the largest number that divides two numbers exactly.
The other of me is the smallest number divisible by both.
We are connected by the formula: HCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b.
For 12 and 18, my two values are 6 and 36.

educationalInfo.definition: HCF (Highest Common Factor) is the largest factor shared by two numbers. LCM (Lowest Common Multiple) is the smallest multiple shared by two numbers.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing HCF with LCM. Using the wrong method (listing vs prime factorisation).
educationalInfo.funFact: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers. This elegant relationship helps quickly find one if you know the other.
practiceQuestions: Find HCF and LCM of 15 and 20.
If HCF(a,b)=6 and LCM(a,b)=72, find a×b.

thoughts: I work with two or more numbers.
I use factors and multiples.
One of me finds the biggest common factor.
The other finds the smallest common multiple.
I help solve number puzzles.

prime_factors.name: Prime Factors
prime_factors.subject: Number
clues: I break a number down into its most fundamental building blocks.
I express any composite number as a product of prime numbers only.
I use a factor tree or repeated division to find my result.
Every whole number greater than 1 has exactly one version of me (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic).
The prime factorisation of 60 is 2² × 3 × 5.

educationalInfo.definition: The process of expressing a composite number as a product of its prime factors.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Stopping the factor tree too early at a composite number. Including 1 as a prime factor.
educationalInfo.funFact: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic guarantees every integer > 1 has a unique prime factorisation — one of the most elegant results in mathematics.
practiceQuestions: Write 90 as a product of prime factors.
Find the prime factorisation of 360.

thoughts: I break numbers into smaller numbers.
My small numbers are all prime.
A factor tree helps me.
12 becomes 2 × 2 × 3.
I show how a number is made.

rounding.name: Rounding
rounding.subject: Number
clues: I approximate a number to a specified degree of precision.
I make large or complex numbers easier to work with.
I can reduce a number to the nearest ten, hundred, or decimal place.
When the digit to my right is 5 or more, I round up.
3.14159... becomes 3.14 when I work to 2 decimal places.

educationalInfo.definition: Approximating a number to a given number of significant figures, decimal places, or nearest value.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Rounding 4.45 to 1 d.p. incorrectly — check the second decimal carefully. Rounding intermediate steps in calculations.
educationalInfo.funFact: GPS systems must round satellite signals to nanoseconds — tiny rounding errors can place you hundreds of metres in the wrong location.
practiceQuestions: Round 4.567 to 2 decimal places.
Round 38,471 to the nearest 1000.

thoughts: I make numbers simpler.
I find the nearest ten or hundred.
If the last digit is 5 or more, I go up.
If it is less than 5, I go down.
100.7 becomes 101 when you use me.
rounding.hint: Look at the digit to the right.

arithmetic.name: Arithmetic
arithmetic.subject: Arithmetic Kingdom
clues: I help you solve everyday number problems.
You have used me since your first maths class.
I include different ways of working with numbers.
I am the foundation of almost every maths topic.
I include addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.
thoughts: I help you solve everyday number problems.
You have used me since your first maths class.
I include different ways of working with numbers.
I am the foundation of almost every maths topic.
I include addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.
hints: Think about the basic operations of mathematics.

educationalInfo.definition: The elementary branch of mathematics that deals with calculations involving numbers using basic operations.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Not paying attention to operational order (BODMAS/PEMDAS) in long calculations.

arithmetic.hint: Recall that Arithmetic refers to: The elementary branch of mathematics that deals with calculations involving numbers using basic operations.

profit_loss.name: Profit & Loss
profit_loss.subject: Arithmetic Kingdom
clues: I am about buying and selling.
Shopkeepers use me every day.
Sometimes you earn money, sometimes you lose money.
I compare the cost price and selling price.
I use CP and SP to find the result.
thoughts: I am about buying and selling.
Shopkeepers use me every day.
Sometimes you earn money, sometimes you lose money.
I compare the cost price and selling price.
I use CP and SP to find the result.

educationalInfo.definition: Financial metric showing gain (Profit = SP - CP) or loss (Loss = CP - SP) incurred in commercial transactions.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Calculating Profit% on Selling Price instead of Cost Price.

profit_loss.hint: Recall that Profit & Loss refers to: Financial metric showing gain (Profit = SP - CP) or loss (Loss = CP - SP) incurred in commercial transactions.

gst.name: GST
gst.subject: Arithmetic Kingdom
clues: I am added when you buy many products.
Governments collect me.
You can find me on bills and receipts.
I am a tax on goods and services.
My amount is usually shown as a %.
thoughts: I am added when you buy many products.
Governments collect me.
You can find me on bills and receipts.
I am a tax on goods and services.
My amount is usually shown as a %.
hints: Think about the tax printed on bills.

educationalInfo.definition: Goods and Services Tax (GST) is an indirect tax levied on the supply of goods and services.
examples: 18% GST on a $100 product adds $18 to total bill ($118 total)
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing exclusive GST (tax added on top) with inclusive GST (tax already included in price).

gst.hint: Recall that GST refers to: Goods and Services Tax (GST) is an indirect tax levied on the supply of goods and services.

banking.name: Recurring Deposit (RD)
banking.subject: Arithmetic Kingdom
clues: I help people save money regularly.
Banks offer me.
You deposit the same amount every month.
I earn interest over time.
People often call me RD.
thoughts: I help people save money regularly.
Banks offer me.
You deposit the same amount every month.
I earn interest over time.
People often call me RD.

educationalInfo.definition: A banking scheme where an individual deposits a fixed monthly amount for a specific period and earns compounding interest.
examples: Depositing $100 every month for 12 months at 6% per annum interest
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Calculating interest as if the full total was deposited on day one.

banking.hint: Recall that Recurring Deposit (RD) refers to: A banking scheme where an individual deposits a fixed monthly amount for a specific period and earns compounding interest.

shares_dividends.name: Shares & Dividends
shares_dividends.subject: Arithmetic Kingdom
clues: I am connected with companies.
People buy a small part of a business through me.
Investors use me to grow their money.
Companies may share part of their profit with owners.
My short forms include EPS and DPS.
thoughts: I am connected with companies.
People buy a small part of a business through me.
Investors use me to grow their money.
Companies may share part of their profit with owners.
My short forms include EPS and DPS.

educationalInfo.definition: Shares represent units of ownership in a corporation; Dividends are profit distributions paid by companies to shareholders.
examples: Owning 100 shares of a company paying $2 dividend per share = $200 income
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing Nominal Value (Face Value) of a share with Market Value.

shares_dividends.hint: Recall that Shares & Dividends refers to: Shares represent units of ownership in a corporation; Dividends are profit distributions paid by companies to shareholders.

speed_distance_time.name: Speed, Distance & Time
speed_distance_time.subject: Arithmetic Kingdom
clues: I describe how people and vehicles travel.
Cars, trains and planes all use me.
Three quantities are connected in me.
If you know any two, you can find the third.
I use the formula Speed = Distance ÷ Time.
thoughts: I describe how people and vehicles travel.
Cars, trains and planes all use me.
Three quantities are connected in me.
If you know any two, you can find the third.
I use the formula Speed = Distance ÷ Time.

educationalInfo.definition: The kinematic relationship relating motion: Speed = Distance / Time, Distance = Speed × Time, Time = Distance / Speed.
examples: Traveling 120 km in 2 hours = Speed of 60 km/h
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Inconsistent units (e.g., mixing km/h with seconds without conversion).

speed_distance_time.hint: Recall that Speed, Distance & Time refers to: The kinematic relationship relating motion: Speed = Distance / Time, Distance = Speed × Time, Time = Distance / Speed.

standard_form.name: Standard Form
standard_form.subject: Arithmetic
clues: I am the way we write numbers in everyday communication.
I combine all place value digits into a single, compact number side-by-side!
Instead of writing 300 + 50 + 4, I write the compact result 354.
Writing your age as 12 or price as 354.
Standard form is writing a number using digits in their standard place value positions.

educationalInfo.definition: Standard form is the standard way of writing numbers using digits (e.g. 354).
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing scientific standard form with elementary standard form.
educationalInfo.funFact: Standard form is the most compact way to write numbers!

standard_form.hint: Recall that Standard Form refers to: Standard form is the standard way of writing numbers using digits (e.

number_bases.name: Number Bases
number_bases.subject: Arithmetic Kingdom
clues: I change the way numbers are written.
Computers use one of my systems every day.
I am not always based on ten.
Binary, octal and hexadecimal belong to me.
My common bases are 2, 8, 10 and 16.
thoughts: I change the way numbers are written.
Computers use one of my systems every day.
I am not always based on ten.
Binary, octal and hexadecimal belong to me.
My common bases are 2, 8, 10 and 16.
hints: Think about different counting systems used in mathematics and computers.

educationalInfo.definition: Positional numeral systems defined by a base number of unique digits (Base-2 Binary, Base-8 Octal, Base-10 Decimal, Base-16 Hexadecimal).
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Using digits equal to or greater than the base (e.g., using digit '2' in Base-2).

number_bases.hint: Recall that Number Bases refers to: Positional numeral systems defined by a base number of unique digits (Base-2 Binary, Base-8 Octal, Base-10 Decimal, Base-16 Hexadecimal).

angles.name: Angles
angles.subject: Geometry
clues: I measure the rotation between two rays sharing a common endpoint.
My unit is the degree, and a full rotation equals 360 of them.
I am acute when less than 90°, obtuse between 90° and 180°.
Vertically opposite versions of me are always equal.
Alternate angles between parallel lines are always equal.

educationalInfo.definition: A measure of the turn between two rays sharing a common vertex, measured in degrees.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing co-interior angles (supplementary) with alternate angles (equal). Measuring with a protractor from the wrong baseline.
educationalInfo.funFact: The Babylonians chose 360° for a full circle because 360 has many divisors — making it easy to divide into equal arcs.
practiceQuestions: Find the missing angle on a straight line if one angle is 73°.
Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Find all 8 angles if one is 55°.

angles.hint: Recall that Angles refers to: A measure of the turn between two rays sharing a common vertex, measured in degrees.

triangles.name: Triangles
triangles.subject: Geometry
clues: I am the simplest polygon, with exactly three sides.
The sum of my interior angles is always exactly 180°.
I can be classified as equilateral, isosceles, or scalene.
My exterior angle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles.
The area of me is half times base times height.

educationalInfo.definition: A three-sided polygon whose interior angles always sum to 180°.
examples: Isosceles: 2 equal sides, 2 equal base angles
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Assuming all triangles have a right angle. Forgetting the exterior angle theorem.
educationalInfo.funFact: Any triangle can tile a flat plane without gaps — a fact used in architecture and Islamic geometric art.
practiceQuestions: Two angles of a triangle are 48° and 73°. Find the third.
Can a triangle have angles 90°, 91°, and -1°?

triangles.hint: Recall that Triangles refers to: A three-sided polygon whose interior angles always sum to 180°.

congruence.name: Congruence
congruence.subject: Geometry
clues: I describe two shapes that are exactly the same size and shape.
I can be established without measuring every single part.
My four main conditions for triangles are SSS, SAS, ASA, and RHS.
If two triangles satisfy any of my conditions, they are identical.
Shapes that satisfy me can be mapped onto each other by rotation, reflection, or translation.

educationalInfo.definition: Two figures are congruent if they have exactly the same shape and size — one can be superimposed on the other.
examples: SAS: two sides and the included angle equal
RHS: right angle, hypotenuse, and one side equal
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing congruence (same size) with similarity (same shape, different size). Using SSA as a congruence condition (it is not reliable).
educationalInfo.funFact: Mass production relies on congruence — every bolt of a given specification is congruent to every other bolt of that size.
practiceQuestions: State the congruence condition for two triangles with equal hypotenuse, right angle, and one leg.
Can two triangles with angles 40°, 60°, 80° be congruent?

congruence.hint: Recall that Congruence refers to: Two figures are congruent if they have exactly the same shape and size — one can be superimposed on the other.

similarity.name: Similarity
similarity.subject: Geometry
clues: I describe shapes that have the same angles but different sizes.
I am related to, but not the same as, congruence.
My scale factor relates the corresponding lengths of two similar figures.
Areas of similar shapes are related by my scale factor squared.
Volumes of similar solids are related by my scale factor cubed.

educationalInfo.definition: Two shapes are similar if they have the same angles and corresponding sides are in proportion.
examples: Scale factor 2: lengths double, area quadruples, volume octuples.
All circles are similar to each other.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Using the scale factor directly for area (must square it) or volume (must cube it).
educationalInfo.funFact: A map is a similarity transformation of real geography — every road, lake, and mountain is a scaled-down replica.
practiceQuestions: Two similar triangles have sides in ratio 3:5. Find the ratio of their areas.
A model car is built at 1:20 scale. If the real car is 4.2m long, how long is the model?

similarity.hint: Recall that Similarity refers to: Two shapes are similar if they have the same angles and corresponding sides are in proportion.

polygons.name: Polygons
polygons.subject: Geometry
clues: I am a closed 2D shape made of straight sides.
My interior angles sum to (n−2) × 180°.
A regular version of me has all sides and angles equal.
A hexagon, octagon, and decagon are all examples of me.
My exterior angles always sum to exactly 360°.

educationalInfo.definition: A closed plane figure bounded by three or more straight sides.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Using the wrong formula for the sum of interior angles. Confusing interior with exterior angles.
educationalInfo.funFact: Honeybees instinctively build hexagonal cells — the regular hexagon packs the most area with the least wax.
practiceQuestions: Find the sum of interior angles of an octagon.
Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 150°. How many sides does it have?

polygons.hint: Recall that Polygons refers to: A closed plane figure bounded by three or more straight sides.

circle_theorems.name: Circle Theorems
circle_theorems.subject: Geometry
clues: I am a collection of rules about angles formed inside and around circles.
One of my rules says the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.
Another of my rules says angles in the same segment are equal.
I state that opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°.
A tangent from an external point creates a right angle with the radius.

educationalInfo.definition: A set of theorems describing angle and chord relationships in and around circles.
examples: Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference
Opposite angles of cyclic quad sum to 180°
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Confusing the inscribed angle theorem with the tangent-radius theorem. Misidentifying the arc the angle stands on.
educationalInfo.funFact: Euclid proved all of these theorems in his Elements around 300 BC — and they still appear on every major exam.
practiceQuestions: An angle at the centre of a circle is 84°. Find the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc.
Prove that the angle in a semicircle is 90°.

circle_theorems.hint: Recall that Circle Theorems refers to: A set of theorems describing angle and chord relationships in and around circles.

herons_formula.name: Heron's Formula
herons_formula.subject: Geometry
clues: I calculate the area of a triangle from its three side lengths alone.
I do not require the height of the triangle.
My formula uses the semi-perimeter, s = (a + b + c) / 2.
My full formula is Area = √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)).
I was discovered by Hero of Alexandria around 60 AD.

educationalInfo.definition: A formula for the area of a triangle with sides a, b, c: Area = √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)) where s = (a+b+c)/2.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting to compute s first. Arithmetic errors inside the square root.
educationalInfo.funFact: Heron's formula is especially useful in surveying — land parcels are often irregular triangles with known side lengths but unknown heights.
practiceQuestions: Find the area of a triangle with sides 7, 8, and 9.
Use Heron's formula to check the area of a right triangle with legs 5 and 12.

herons_formula.hint: Recall that Heron's Formula refers to: A formula for the area of a triangle with sides a, b, c: Area = √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)) where s = (a+b+c)/2.

circular_measure.name: Circular Measure
circular_measure.subject: Geometry
clues: I express angles in a unit other than degrees.
My unit is the radian, defined as the angle subtended at the centre by an arc equal to the radius.
A full circle contains exactly 2π of my units.
180° equals π of my units.
Arc length = radius × angle in my units; sector area = ½r²θ.

educationalInfo.definition: Measurement of angles in radians, where 1 radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Forgetting to convert degrees to radians before using arc/sector formulae. Using degrees in radian formulas.
educationalInfo.funFact: Radians make calculus formulas for trigonometry clean — without them, derivatives of sin and cos would have extra π/180 factors.
practiceQuestions: Convert 120° to radians.
Find the arc length of a sector with radius 5 cm and angle π/3 rad.

circular_measure.hint: Recall that Circular Measure refers to: Measurement of angles in radians, where 1 radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius.

transformations.name: Transformations
transformations.subject: Geometry
clues: I describe ways of moving or changing a shape without altering its basic structure.
My four main types are translation, reflection, rotation, and enlargement.
A translation moves every point by the same vector.
A reflection flips a shape over a mirror line.
An enlargement scales a shape from a centre point by a scale factor.

educationalInfo.definition: A transformation changes the position, orientation, or size of a shape. Types: translation, reflection, rotation, enlargement.
examples: Translation by (3,−2): every point moves 3 right, 2 down.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Applying the wrong rotation rule. Forgetting that enlargement also has a centre, not just a scale factor.
educationalInfo.funFact: The symmetric patterns in Islamic geometric art use all four transformations — created without modern algebra purely by geometric intuition.
practiceQuestions: Reflect the point (3,4) in the x-axis.
Describe fully the transformation that maps triangle A to triangle B.

transformations.hint: Recall that Transformations refers to: A transformation changes the position, orientation, or size of a shape.

simultaneous_equations.name: Simultaneous Equations
simultaneous_equations.subject: Algebra
clues: I am a system of two or more equations that must all be true at the same time.
My solution is the set of values that satisfies every equation simultaneously.
I can be solved by substitution or by elimination.
Graphically, my solution is the point where two lines intersect.
For 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2, my solution is x=3, y=1.

educationalInfo.definition: A set of equations with multiple unknowns that must be solved together to find a common solution.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Sign errors when subtracting equations. Substituting back into only one equation without checking the other.
educationalInfo.funFact: Ancient Chinese mathematicians solved systems of linear equations in their book 'The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art' around 200 BC.
practiceQuestions: Solve: 3x + 2y = 16 and x − y = 1.
Solve by substitution: y = 2x − 3 and 4x + y = 9.

simultaneous_equations.hint: Recall that Simultaneous Equations refers to: A set of equations with multiple unknowns that must be solved together to find a common solution.

indices.name: Indices
indices.subject: Algebra
clues: I govern the laws of exponents and powers.
My first law: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ.
My second law: aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ.
A negative me means a reciprocal: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
A fractional me means a root: a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a.

educationalInfo.definition: The laws governing exponents (powers), including multiplication, division, power of a power, negative, and fractional exponents.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Adding bases instead of exponents when multiplying. Applying power rules to sums (e.g. (a+b)² ≠ a²+b²).
educationalInfo.funFact: Fractional indices elegantly unify powers and roots — the same notation covers both with a single rule.
practiceQuestions: Simplify: x³ × x⁴ ÷ x².
Evaluate 8^(2/3).

indices.hint: Recall that Indices refers to: The laws governing exponents (powers), including multiplication, division, power of a power, negative, and fractional exponents.

surds.name: Surds
surds.subject: Algebra
clues: I am an irrational number expressed as a root that cannot be simplified to a whole number.
I appear when square roots of non-perfect-square numbers are not simplified away.
√2, √3, and √5 are examples of me.
I can be simplified: √12 = 2√3.
Rationalising the denominator removes me from the bottom of a fraction.

educationalInfo.definition: An irrational number in root form that cannot be expressed as a simple fraction, e.g. √2, ∛5.
educationalInfo.commonMistakes: Thinking √(a+b) = √a + √b. Forgetting to rationalise the denominator when required.
